short: Wyoming has no dedicated AI act, but a 2026 law criminalizes AI-generated child exploitation material, and existing consumer protection, data breach, and insurance statutes already reach AI-driven conduct in the state.
title: Wyoming AI Laws
subtitle: What actually applies to AI in Wyoming, from failed deepfake bills to the consumer protection and insurance laws already in force
body_html:
Wyoming has no dedicated AI act. Lawmakers spent two years drafting broad AI governance bills and could not agree on them, but the 2026 legislature passed a narrower criminal law covering AI-generated child exploitation material and other AI-enabled harms, and several existing consumer protection, insurance, and criminal statutes already reach a wide range of AI conduct in the state.

What the legislature did

Wyoming's first attempt at AI legislation was Senate File 51 in the 2024 budget session, "Unlawful dissemination of misleading synthetic media." It would have banned distributing deepfakes meant to mislead and required disclaimers on AI-altered content. It passed the Senate 17-7 on February 27, 2024, but died in the House Corporations Committee on March 5, after Rep. Ocean Andrew argued it would "unconstitutionally hinder a person's freedom of speech" and Sen. Affie Ellis called it overly broad.

The Legislature's Select Committee on Blockchain, Financial Technology and Digital Innovation Technology, co-chaired by Sen. Chris Rothfuss and Rep. Cyrus Western, tried again in the 2024 interim with Bill Draft 149, a revised SF 51, and Bill Draft 150, limited to synthetic media of election candidates. Neither reached a floor vote. The committee could not reach unanimous agreement at its July 2024 meeting in Sheridan and set both aside indefinitely by September over First Amendment concerns, so no synthetic media bill was introduced in the 2025 general session.

In 2025 the Joint Labor, Health and Social Services interim committee examined whether insurers should be barred from using AI to deny health claims, hearing testimony about an out-of-state lawsuit against UnitedHealth over AI-driven Medicare Advantage denials. Lawmakers declined to add AI-specific language, reasoning it might create loopholes for insurers, and left in place a 2024 law requiring licensed physicians to review adverse claim determinations.

The 2026 budget session produced Wyoming's first enacted AI-specific statute. House Bill 102, "Protecting kids from deepfakes and exploitative images," sponsored by Rep. Jayme Lien, criminalizes using AI to generate child sexual abuse material or nonconsensual intimate deepfakes, states that using AI to commit a crime is not a legal defense, criminalizes using AI to promote self-harm or censor political speech, and grants limited immunity to AI developers under specified conditions. It passed the House 61-0-1 and the Senate 31-0-0, and was signed into law March 7, 2026, as Chapter 91.

What already applies without a dedicated AI act

The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act (W.S. 40-12-101 et seq.) prohibits unfair or deceptive trade practices and is enforced by the Attorney General's Consumer Protection and Antitrust Unit. It does not care whether the deception was produced by a person or an AI system, so a business using an AI chatbot, fake reviews, or AI-written marketing to mislead consumers is already exposed under this statute.

Wyoming's data breach notification law (W.S. 40-12-501 et seq.) requires notice when personal identifying information is compromised, and applies to breaches of AI training or operational data the same as any other breach. Wyoming has no comprehensive consumer data privacy act (a 2022 interim draft never became a bill) and no dedicated biometric information privacy statute, so biometric data used in facial recognition or voice AI tools is governed only by these general laws.

On insurance, the 2024 Ensuring Transparency in Prior Authorization Act requires a licensed healthcare professional, not an algorithm alone, to make and review adverse coverage determinations. The Department of Insurance has said it can act against insurers that misuse AI in claims handling under this authority, though Wyoming has not adopted the NAIC's model bulletin on insurer use of AI, unlike roughly two dozen other states. General criminal statutes on fraud, harassment, stalking, and identity theft also apply regardless of whether AI tools were used to commit the offense.

What the Attorney General has done

No AI-specific consumer alert, guidance, or enforcement action from the Wyoming Attorney General's office was found. The Consumer Protection and Antitrust Unit continues to handle complaints under the general Consumer Protection Act, with recent public alerts on vehicle scams and a Meta privacy settlement rather than AI. That does not put AI-driven deception outside the office's authority, it simply has not issued AI-focused public guidance yet.

What this means

Wyoming is not an unregulated state for AI, it regulates AI conduct through existing law rather than a single AI statute. Assume the Consumer Protection Act reaches deceptive AI-generated content, that breach notice duties apply to AI training and operational data, that insurers using AI in claims decisions still need licensed human review of denials, and that generating AI-based child exploitation material or nonconsensual intimate imagery is now a specific felony under Chapter 91. Broader AI governance, on transparency, bias, and automated decision-making, remains unresolved after two years of failed attempts, so expect the Legislature to keep revisiting it.
